original_summary: Ys is a 2-4 player, 4-round majority game. Players bid brokers to set turn order, then take turns placing valued brokers (0-4), face up or face down, into neighborhood areas and a market grid. Majorities award gems, instant points and character cards, and the market moves gem prices that are scored at the end.

review.evidence: Majorities are contested and placement order matters. No single placement policy dominates, because concentrating loses breadth and spreading loses majorities. Turn order gives some seat edge, but it is bid for.
Ship and character draws add variance, but bluffing with face-down brokers, reading opponents' commitments and steering gem prices reward skill over 4 rounds.
Deep interplay between majorities, market prices and bluffs. Weak players still collect some gems.
Face-down broker values hide state. Players must infer true majorities and opponents' gem interests from partial information.
Every result is arithmetic: sums of broker values, ranks, gem counts times prices.

It uses a physical board with a market grid (row and column intersections) and 4 neighborhoods of 3 sub-areas each. It has 10 sequential placements per player per round, several decks (ships, market, characters, order cards) and character powers. This far exceeds 4 choice steps per round and 1 random draw per round, and relies on spatial row/column layout.

problems: Ten sequential broker placements per player per round far exceed the choice-step limit.
The market grid (rows intersecting columns) is a spatial board structure.
Several random decks per round (ships, market card, characters) exceed one random draw per round and add luck.
Character cards with special powers create long rule chains and many attributes.
Face-down brokers create a large amount of hidden state (many hidden elements).
Turn-order bidding plus sequential placement gives later or earlier seats structural edges that need a tie-break deck.
The 2-player version reduces to a pure difference contest in which denial dominates.

changes.what: Replace sequential broker placement with one simultaneous secret allocation: each player splits 6 broker strength among 4 districts.
changes.why: Keeps blind majority bidding and its bluff-by-concealment in a single choice step.
changes.fixes: Ten sequential broker placements per player per round far exceed the choice-step limit.

changes.what: Replace the market grid with a simultaneous market vote: each player names one gem color, each vote raises that color's price by 1, and colors receiving no vote drop by 1 (minimum 1).
changes.why: Keeps price manipulation without any row/column structure.
changes.fixes: The market grid (rows intersecting columns) is a spatial board structure.

changes.what: Remove the ship, market and character decks. Districts always offer fixed rewards. The only randomness is a one-time secret deal of each player's favored color.
changes.why: Removes per-round luck and keeps random draws at 0 per round.
changes.fixes: Several random decks per round (ships, market card, characters) exceed one random draw per round and add luck.

changes.what: Drop character cards. The palace is replaced by a Commerce district that pays flat points.
changes.why: Cuts rule chains while keeping a non-gem majority option like Ys's commercial area.
changes.fixes: Character cards with special powers create long rule chains and many attributes.

changes.what: Use ONE hidden element: each player's secret favored color, whose gems score double. Allocations are revealed after each round.
changes.why: Bluffing is now about hiding which color you truly want. Opponents must infer it from bids and votes in order to avoid raising your color.
changes.fixes: Face-down brokers create a large amount of hidden state (many hidden elements).

changes.what: Make all choices simultaneous and drop turn order.
changes.why: Removes seat advantage and the tie-break deck.
changes.fixes: Turn-order bidding plus sequential placement gives later or earlier seats structural edges that need a tie-break deck.

changes.what: Fix the player count at 3, one secret color per player, with colors dealt as a random permutation.
changes.why: Three players mean a rival's gain is not purely your loss. Symmetric types mean no player is dealt a better type.
changes.fixes: The 2-player version reduces to a pure difference contest in which denial dominates.

keeps: Blind majority bidding of broker strength across neighborhoods
Top ranks in each neighborhood earn colored gems
A commercial majority that pays instant points
A market that players push to change gem values scored at the end
Bluffing about which gems you really want
End scoring of gems times market price

recommendation.reason: The core of Ys (blind majorities, gem collection and market price manipulation with bluffing) survives as a compact simultaneous allocation game within the limits.

variation.name: Ys: Brokers of the Blind Market
variation.summary: Three brokers secretly split their influence across three gem districts and a Commerce district each round, then vote to push gem prices. Each broker secretly favors one color whose gems score double, so the game turns on hiding your color while inferring and undercutting the others'.
variation.rules:
SETUP: There are three gem colors: Red, Blue and Green. Each color's price starts at 3. Before round 1, the three colors are dealt randomly, one to each player, as that player's SECRET FAVORED COLOR. Every player has a different color, and each player knows only their own. All players start with 0 gems of each color and 0 commerce points. The game lasts 6 rounds.

EACH ROUND:
1. Announce. The round number and the current prices of Red, Blue and Green are shown to all.
2. Talk. Everyone writes one short message at the same time without seeing the others. All messages are then shown. Talk is not binding.
3. Allocate (simultaneous, secret). Each player submits four whole numbers, each 0 or more, summing to exactly 6: their influence in the Red district, the Blue district, the Green district and the Commerce district.
4. Reveal. All allocations are shown to everyone.
5. Resolve each of the four districts separately:
   - If one player has the strictly highest influence (above 0), they win FIRST. Otherwise, all players tied at the highest value (above 0) each count as tied-first.
   - If there is a single first, the player with the strictly next-highest influence (above 0) wins SECOND. Second is not awarded if there is a tie for it, or if first was tied.
   - In a gem district, a single first gains 2 gems of that color, second gains 1 gem, and each tied-first gains 1 gem.
   - In Commerce, a single first gains 8 commerce points, second gains 3, and each tied-first gains 3.
   - A player with 0 influence in a district gains nothing there.
6. Market vote (simultaneous). Each player names one color: Red, Blue or Green.
7. Price update. Each color's price rises by 1 for every vote it received. Each color that received 0 votes falls by 1, but never below 1. The votes are then shown.
8. End check. After round 6 the game ends.

FINAL SCORING: Each player's score is the sum over the three colors of (gems of that color × that color's final price). Then add (gems of their secret favored color × that color's final price) again, so favored gems count double. Then add their commerce points. Secret colors are revealed at the end.
variation.objective: The player with the highest final score wins. If two or three players tie for the highest score, the game is a draw.
variation.expected_effect: Players disagree about which gem prices should rise, because each secretly wants their own color high and the others' low. Talk therefore invites bluffing ('Blue is worth pushing'), and a player who just follows a proposal may raise a rival's favored color, handing that rival the win. Heavy, obvious investment in one color reveals your type and invites rivals to contest that district at a tie (6 vs 6) or starve its price with their votes. Concealing is not free either: spending on decoy colors or Commerce costs gems. Simple policies can all lose. 'All 6 on my color' is tied and denied by a rival and its price is starved. 'Always Commerce' caps out near 48 points against gem totals that can exceed it. 'Always vote my color' reveals the color. Types are symmetric, so the deal decides what to do, not who is ahead.

balanced.evidence:
PER-DISTRICT AWARDS: gem district: single first 2 gems, second 1, each tied-first 1. Commerce: 8 / 3 / 3. Prices start at 3 and each round's three votes add +3 in total. If each player votes their own favored color, every price ends at 3+6=9, so a favored gem is worth 18 and any other gem 9. Even at the starting price of 3, a first in your favored district (2 gems × 3 × 2 = 12) beats a Commerce first (8). Commerce only competes if prices fall to about 2 or below, which needs coordinated votes, so it is a weak option, not a dominant one.

THOUGHTLESS POLICIES, judged by the winner rule:
(a) ALL-6-COMMERCE (always last option): 8 per round, 48 total. An opponent putting 6 in its favored district gets 12 favored gems × 18 = 216. All-Commerce loses to sensible play and to most random play (random allocations still win gems worth about 9 each).
(b) ALL-6-IN-ONE-DISTRICT (always highest / always first option, e.g. 6 Red): this guarantees at least tied-first there and nothing elsewhere. Against a spreader P playing Fav 1 / other 1 / other 1 / Commerce 3, where the other players go all-in on their own colors: P wins 2 favored gems (sole entrant in its district), second in both other districts (1 gem each) and the Commerce first (8). Per round P gets 2×18 + 2×9 + 8 = 62 against 36 for each all-in player. All-in loses. When the first option is not the player's favored color, it does even worse.
(c) EVEN SPREAD 2/2/2/0: beats all-in players (2 favored + 2 seconds), but loses to 3/3-style concentration on its favored and contested districts and to a Commerce-plus-favored split. This is Blotto-like non-transitivity.

No allocation is strictly better against every opponent profile. No pure policy never loses.

SEATS: all choices are simultaneous and the colors are interchangeable (equal starting prices, equal rules), so no seat or color has an edge. All three players can win. The game makes no labelled payoff ordering claim to check. Voting for your own favored color is the natural choice, but it is not dominant for winning: a vote also raises the value of opponents' holdings of that color, and denying votes to a leader's color can be decisive.

playable.evidence:
COMPLETENESS: the tie and second-place rules are fully specified: strict highest wins first; a tie at the top means all tied are tied-first; second needs a single first and a strict, untied next-highest above 0. Zero influence earns nothing. Price changes are fully specified, including the floor of 1. Final scoring is pure arithmetic on gems, prices and commerce points. The game is finite at 6 rounds. No judge, board or clock is needed.

LIMITS: steps per round about 12 (announce, talk, allocate, reveal, 4 district resolutions, vote, price update, reveal votes, end check) ≤ 20. Choice steps 3 ≤ 4. Hidden elements 1 ≤ 3. Random draws per round 0; the color deal is a setup draw. Rounds 6 ≤ 40.

ATTRIBUTES: the stated 10 is understated. The real count is 3 prices + 3 players × (3 gem counts + commerce + favored color) = 18. That is still ≤ 20, so this is a documentation error, not a failure.

TALK: the game has 3 players with genuinely conflicting interests. Players disagree over who contests which district and over which colors to vote up or starve. Talk is simultaneous, then all choose. So talk is correctly present.

No trading, binding agreements or conditional blocks are used. Per-district resolution uses conditional per-step scoring, which is supported. The repeated game has no prisoner's-dilemma structure whose late rounds collapse to a safe option.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
CHANCE: the only random element is the favored-color deal. Colors are symmetric (same starting price, same rules), so the deal gives no player an advantage. Chance's share of the result is close to 0%.

GOOD PLAY BY ALL: if all three play the same symmetric strategy (e.g. all-in on their own color, vote own), they draw at 216 each. The deal does not decide the winner. Outcomes come from out-predicting the other players' allocations.

WHAT THERE IS TO INFER:
- Opponents' favored colors, from talk, allocations and votes. The secret leaks within about 1–2 rounds, so hidden information is short-lived.
- The main ongoing inference is opponent modelling in a 3-player Blotto: where will others concentrate, where can a 1-point entry take second, and when is it worth contesting a rival's favored district to cut its gems from 2 to 1 (tie) or zero.
- Vote targeting: starve the leader's color.

PLANNING: final prices are what count. Late votes and the accumulated gem mix call for multi-round planning.

A reasoning player clearly beats a thoughtless one: in the per-round example above, 62 against 36.
